chapter.name: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market

questions.q: Differentiate between individual demand and market demand, using the prices Rs 150, Rs 100 and Rs 50 of the chapter's mango table.
questions.a: Individual demand is what one buyer wants at different prices, keeping other factors constant, e.g. Srivalli 1, 2, 3 kg. Market demand is the total quantity all potential buyers want at each price, e.g. 6, 12, 18 kg for the three buyers.
s: Individual demand: one buyer, with a figure for her
Market demand: the sum over all buyers, with the figures 6, 12 and 18 kg

questions.q: Srivalli buys 2 kg of mangoes at Rs 100 per kg. If three buyers with exactly the same schedule as hers make up a market, the market demand at Rs 100 is ___ kg.

Create your own demand schedule for notebooks at Rs 20, Rs 40 and Rs 60 for yourself and two friends, with the quantity each of you would buy. Find the market demand at each price, say at which price the market demand is highest and explain what would make one of you stop buying altogether.
questions.a: Any consistent schedule in which each person's quantity falls as price rises, e.g. 6, 4, 2 for one person. The market demand is the sum for the three at each price, highest at the lowest price (Rs 20). A person stops buying when the price is more than she is willing to pay or more than she can afford (purchasing power), as the chapter says demand depends on both.
s: A schedule for three people in which quantity falls as price rises
Market demand totals correct and highest at Rs 20
Stopping point linked to willingness and purchasing power

questions.q:
The tuck shop of a school sells samosas. Classes 9A, 9B and 9C together buy 20, 25 and 15 samosas a day at Rs 10 each. When the price is Rs 15 they buy 14, 16 and 10, and at Rs 20 they buy 8, 10 and 6. Each samosa costs the shop Rs 6 to make. The principal wants as many students as possible to be able to buy, but the shop must also cover its costs.
(a) Find the total daily demand at each price.
(b) Does the total follow the Law of Demand? Say how you know.
(c) Work out the shop's sales revenue at each price.
(d) Work out the profit (revenue minus the Rs 6 cost of every samosa sold) at each price and recommend a price, saying clearly what your choice gives up.
questions.a: (a) 60, 40 and 24. (b) Yes: the quantity falls from 60 to 40 to 24 as the price rises from Rs 10 to Rs 15 to Rs 20, an inverse relationship. (c) Revenue Rs 600, Rs 600 and Rs 480. (d) Profit is 60 x 4 = Rs 240, 40 x 9 = Rs 360 and 24 x 14 = Rs 336. Rs 15 gives the most profit but serves 20 fewer samosas a day than Rs 10; Rs 10 serves most students with a lower profit. Either choice is acceptable if the trade-off is named.
s: (a) Totals 60, 40 and 24
(b) Inverse relationship recognised with the figures
(c) Revenues Rs 600, Rs 600 and Rs 480
(d) Profits Rs 240, Rs 360 and Rs 336 and a recommendation naming what is given up

questions.q: Alex's schedule is 2 kg at Rs 150, 4 kg at Rs 100 and 6 kg at Rs 50. Srivalli's is 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg at the same prices. (a) How much more than Srivalli does Alex buy at Rs 50? (b) When the price falls from Rs 150 to Rs 50, by how much does each of them increase the quantity bought, and what does the comparison show?
questions.a: (a) 6 - 3 = 3 kg more. (b) Alex increases by 6 - 2 = 4 kg and Srivalli by 3 - 1 = 2 kg. Both buy more as the price falls, Alex by twice as much, so the same price fall gives a different response for different buyers.
s: (a) Difference at Rs 50 worked out as 3 kg
(b) Increases of 4 kg and 2 kg, with the comparison: both obey the law, Alex responds more

questions.q: Which pair of points can lie on one and the same individual demand curve, when income, taste and the other factors are kept constant?
questions.a: On an individual demand curve each price has one quantity, and a lower price goes with a larger quantity, as at Rs 150 for 1 kg and Rs 50 for 3 kg.
o: Rs 150 with 1 kg, and Rs 50 with 3 kg
Rs 150 with 3 kg, and Rs 50 with 1 kg
Rs 100 with 2 kg, and Rs 100 with 5 kg
Rs 50 with 3 kg, and Rs 150 with 3 kg

questions.q: Use the chapter's table of Srivalli, Alex and Israt. (i) Find the market demand at Rs 150, Rs 100 and Rs 50. (ii) Show that the individual and the market demand both obey the Law of Demand. (iii) Explain why the market curve is flatter than Srivalli's. (iv) Amit wants 4 kg of mangoes at Rs 150 but has only Rs 100 with him. Explain whether he adds to the market demand at that price.
questions.a: (i) 6, 12 and 18 kg. (ii) Srivalli goes 1, 2, 3 kg and the market 6, 12, 18 kg as the price falls; both rise as price falls. (iii) The market adds many consumers, so the same price fall gives a larger total response (12 kg against 2 kg). (iv) Amit has willingness but not the purchasing power to buy 4 kg at Rs 150, so he does not add to the demand at that price.
s: Market demand totals worked out
Both obey the inverse relationship, with figures
Flatter market curve explained by adding many consumers
Amit: willingness without purchasing power is not demand

questions.q: Divya wants a Rs 9,000 phone very badly, but she has saved only Rs 800 and has no other source of money. Using the chapter's meaning of demand, what should we say about her at the price of Rs 9,000?
questions.a: Demand is willingness complemented by the ability, or purchasing power, to buy. Divya has the willingness but not the purchasing power at that price.
o: She has the wish but not the purchasing power, so this is not her demand
She wants it strongly, so her demand at that price is one phone
Her demand is decided only by the price of the phone, not by her money
Her demand will arise only when the phone is on sale in a particular season

questions.q: Raju buys 5, 8 and 12 notebooks at Rs 40, Rs 30 and Rs 20, and his sister buys 2, 4 and 6 at the same prices. Work out the market demand at each price, find the price at which it is 18 notebooks and say whether the pattern obeys the law of demand.
questions.a: Market demand is 7 at Rs 40, 12 at Rs 30 and 18 at Rs 20. It is 18 notebooks at Rs 20. Quantity rises as price falls, so the law of demand is obeyed.
s: Totals 7, 12 and 18 worked out
Price for 18 notebooks: Rs 20
Pattern obeys the inverse relationship

questions.q:
Read these statements about demand.
1. Demand is the willingness to buy complemented by the ability, or purchasing power, to buy.
2. An individual demand curve is drawn on the assumption that income and taste keep changing along with the price.
3. Market demand at a price is the total of all the individual demands at that price.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 is false: the curve is drawn assuming income, taste and other factors are constant. Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: (a) State the Law of Demand. (b) A trader says, 'Last week I raised the price of guavas from Rs 50 to Rs 80 and my sales went up, so the law of demand is wrong.' Give one reason, based on the chapter, why this does not disprove the law.
questions.a: (a) When the price of a product rises, the quantity demanded decreases, and when it falls the quantity demanded increases: an inverse relationship. (b) The law holds with other factors such as income and taste constant; if something else changed that week (a festival, a rise in income, a change in taste), the sales rise need not come from the price.
s: (a) The inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded
(b) The law assumes other factors are constant, so another change could explain the sales

questions.q: Rohit says, 'Srivalli's demand follows the law of demand, and market demand is only the total of the individuals, so the market demand curve must slope downward as well.' Is he right? Check with the chapter's three-buyer table.
questions.a: Yes, he is right. The market demand is 6 kg at Rs 150, 12 kg at Rs 100 and 18 kg at Rs 50. It rises each time the price falls, so the market demand curve also slopes downward and shows the inverse relationship.
s: Verdict: yes
Market demand figures 6, 12 and 18 kg read off correctly
Conclusion: quantity rises as price falls, so the curve slopes downward

questions.q: Describe how Srivalli's demand schedule is turned into her demand curve. Say what each axis shows and name the three points.
questions.a: Price is plotted on the y-axis and quantity on the x-axis. The schedule gives three points: A (1 kg, Rs 150), B (2 kg, Rs 100) and C (3 kg, Rs 50). Joining A, B and C gives the downward-sloping line DD', the demand curve.
s: Axes: price on y, quantity on x
The three points A, B and C with their values
Joining them gives the downward-sloping demand curve DD'

questions.q: When the price falls from Rs 150 to Rs 50, Srivalli buys 2 kg more. The three buyers together buy 12 kg more. Explain what this shows about the market demand curve compared with Srivalli's curve.
questions.a: The market demand curve is flatter and more responsive than the individual curve. Market demand adds up many consumers, so the same price change produces a larger total change in quantity.
s: The market curve is flatter and more responsive
Reason: many consumers are added, so the same price change gives a larger total response

questions.q:
Match each description with the term it fits.
1. A table of the kilograms Srivalli buys at Rs 150, Rs 100 and Rs 50
2. The downward-sloping line DD' through the points A, B and C
3. The quantities of Srivalli, Alex and Israt added together at each price
4. A student who wants a phone but has no means to pay for it
a. Market demand
b. Demand schedule
c. Demand curve
d. Willingness without purchasing power, so not demand
questions.a: The table is a demand schedule (b); the line through A, B, C is the demand curve (c); the added quantities are market demand (a); wanting without the means to pay is not demand (d).

questions.q: A shopkeeper records guava sales on three days. Which record fits a demand schedule that obeys the Law of Demand, with other factors unchanged?
questions.a: Only the record in which the quantity bought rises as the price falls shows the inverse relationship of the Law of Demand.
o: Rs 60 sells 4 kg, Rs 40 sells 7 kg, Rs 20 sells 11 kg
Rs 60 sells 11 kg, Rs 40 sells 7 kg, Rs 20 sells 4 kg
Rs 60 sells 7 kg, Rs 40 sells 7 kg, Rs 20 sells 7 kg
Rs 60 sells 4 kg, Rs 40 sells 11 kg, Rs 20 sells 7 kg

questions.q: True or False: A household's demand for a product depends only on the price of that product, not on its income or on the prices of other goods.
questions.a: False. The chapter lists other determinants of demand, such as income, tastes and the prices of related goods (substitutes, complements). The price moves us along the demand curve; these others shift it.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: income, tastes and related goods' prices also determine demand

questions.q: Three buyers' purchases of mangoes at Rs 100 per kg are 2 kg, 4 kg and 6 kg. A fourth buyer, Dev, who wants 5 kg at that price, joins the market. What is the market demand at Rs 100 now?
questions.a: Market demand is the sum of all individual demands: 2 + 4 + 6 + 5 = 17 kg.
o: 17 kg
12 kg
5 kg
24 kg

questions.q:
Three households in a colony buy mangoes from a vendor. At Rs 150 per kg they buy 1, 2 and 3 kg; at Rs 100 they buy 2, 4 and 6 kg; at Rs 50 they buy 3, 6 and 9 kg. A fourth household, the Josephs, moves in and wants 1 kg at Rs 150, 3 kg at Rs 100 and 4 kg at Rs 50. The vendor, who has 20 kg for the day, says, 'At Rs 50 I sell the most mangoes, so Rs 50 must be my best price.'
(a) Find the new market demand at each of the three prices.
(b) By how much does the market demand increase when the price falls from Rs 150 to Rs 50, and how does that compare with the increase before the Josephs came?
(c) Why does adding the Josephs make the market curve even more responsive than a single buyer's curve?
(d) Is the vendor right that Rs 50 is her best price? Compare her sales revenue at the three prices, remembering that she has only 20 kg.
questions.a: (a) 7, 15 and 22 kg. (b) 22 - 7 = 15 kg now, against 18 - 6 = 12 kg before. (c) More consumers are added, so the same price fall gives a larger total response. (d) Revenue at Rs 150 is 7 x 150 = Rs 1,050; at Rs 100 it is 15 x 100 = Rs 1,500; at Rs 50 she sells only her 20 kg, which gives Rs 1,000. She sells the most at Rs 50, but the best revenue is at Rs 100, so selling more is not the same as earning more.
s: (a) Totals 7, 15 and 22 kg
(b) Increase of 15 kg against 12 kg before
(c) More buyers added, so larger total response to the same price change
(d) Revenue Rs 1,050, Rs 1,500 and Rs 1,000 compared; selling most is not the best revenue

questions.q:
Assertion (A): At Rs 50 per kg, Srivalli buys 3 kg of mangoes, while the market demand in the chapter's table is 18 kg.
Reason (R): Market demand is the sum of the quantities that all the consumers want to buy at that price.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true: 3 + 6 + 9 = 18 kg at Rs 50. The market figure is bigger because it adds up all three buyers, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: When the price of coffee rises and many drinkers shift to tea, tea and coffee are called ___ goods.
questions.a: substitute

Read these statements about the factors that influence demand.
1. If the price of a substitute rises, the demand for the other good falls.
2. If demand for printers rises, the demand for printer cartridges may also rise even though the cartridge price is unchanged.
3. If consumers expect prices to fall, they postpone purchases, decreasing present demand.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: if the price of a substitute rises, the demand for the other good rises. Statements 2 and 3 are from the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q: A new smartphone model is launched and long queues form even though it is costly. (i) Explain what the queue shows about the idea that demand depends only on price. (ii) Using earphones as the example, explain how its launch can affect the demand for another good. (iii) Name two more factors that could raise the demand for the phone and explain each in one line.
questions.a: (i) The queue shows demand does not change only because of price; other factors such as taste, income and trend also matter. (ii) Smartphones and earphones are complementary goods, so higher demand for phones raises demand for earphones. (iii) Any two of: rising incomes (people can afford more), tastes and preferences (liking for the brand), festival season or expectation that prices will rise soon.
s: (i) Demand is influenced by factors beyond price
(ii) Complementary goods, with earphones' demand rising
(iii) Two further factors each explained

questions.q: True or False: When household income rises, the quantity demanded of several goods generally rises even if their prices stay the same.
questions.a: True. The chapter says rising income lets consumers buy more or choose higher-quality products and makes people more confident about spending.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: higher income gives more purchasing power and confidence to spend

questions.q:
A footwear shop in a town of 12,000 people studies who buys what. Thirty per cent of the residents are children, who buy 2 pairs of sports shoes a year each at Rs 800 a pair. Half are working adults, who buy 1 pair of formal shoes a year each at Rs 1,500. The rest are elderly people, who buy 1 pair of orthopaedic shoes a year each at Rs 2,200. A factory then closes and 1,500 working adults leave the town.
(a) How many pairs of each kind does the town buy in a year before the factory closes?
(b) Which part of the population-based demand falls after the closure, and by how many pairs?
(c) Find the yearly sales value of each kind of shoe after the closure.
(d) The owner can give extra shelf space to only one kind. Which would you choose and what does your choice leave behind?
questions.a: (a) Sports 7,200 pairs; formal 6,000; orthopaedic 2,400. (b) Formal shoes fall by 1,500 pairs to 4,500, since the working adults who buy them have gone. (c) Sports 7,200 x 800 = Rs 57,60,000; formal 4,500 x 1,500 = Rs 67,50,000; orthopaedic 2,400 x 2,200 = Rs 52,80,000. (d) Formal shoes still bring the highest value despite the fall, while sports shoes sell the most pairs; the chapter's point is that the make-up of the population shapes demand. Either choice is acceptable if the trade-off of value against number of buyers is named.
s: (b) Formal shoes, down by 1,500 pairs
(d) A choice justified by value or buyers, with the trade-off named

questions.q: Write a situation from your own town in which the demand for a good changes although its price stays the same. Name the factor and say whether demand rises or falls.
questions.a: Any valid situation, e.g. before Rakhi, demand for sweets rises with no price change (seasonality: festivals); or families postpone buying a phone because they expect a price cut (expectations, demand falls).
s: A realistic situation with no change in the good's own price
The correct factor named
The direction of change matches the factor

questions.q: Exercise 1 of the chapter says, 'An increase in income always leads to a rise in demand for goods.' How far is this right?
questions.a: Partly right. The chapter says rising income generally raises the quantity demanded of several goods, since people can afford more or buy better. But 'always' goes beyond the chapter, which says 'generally' and 'several goods', and tastes and other factors also decide what people buy.
s: Verdict: partly right
The right part: income generally raises demand for several goods
The 'always' is too strong: other factors such as taste also matter

questions.q: Coffee rises from Rs 40 to Rs 60 a cup, while tea stays at Rs 20 a cup. Kiran says, 'Tea has not changed in price, so the demand for tea cannot change.' What does the chapter's idea of related goods say?
questions.a: Tea and coffee are substitutes. When the price of one rises people switch to the cheaper alternative, so demand for tea can increase even though its own price is unchanged.
o: Tea demand can rise, since people shift from costlier coffee to tea
Tea demand must stay the same, since the price of tea has not changed
Tea demand falls, since both drinks are hot and sold together as a pair
Tea demand falls, since coffee has become costlier for coffee drinkers

questions.q: A survey shows that the number of children in a town has grown a lot, while the number of working adults and elderly people has stayed the same. According to the chapter, which product is most likely to see a rise in demand?
questions.a: The chapter says the composition of the population shapes demand: more children indicate increased demand for sports shoes.
o: Sports shoes
Formal shoes
Orthopaedic shoes
None of these, since only the size of a population affects demand

questions.q: A company cuts the price of printers and the sales of printers rise. (a) Name the kind of related goods that printers and cartridges are. (b) The price of cartridges stays unchanged; what happens to the demand for cartridges, and why?
questions.a: (a) Complementary goods. (b) The demand for cartridges rises, because the goods are used together, so more printers in use means more demand for cartridges.
s: (a) Complementary goods
(b) Demand for cartridges rises, with the reason that they are used with printers

questions.q: Petrol prices double. Using the ideas of complementary and substitute goods, say what you expect to happen to (i) the demand for petrol cars, (ii) the demand for car accessories, and (iii) the demand for public transport, giving one reason each.
questions.a: (i) Demand for petrol cars falls, since cars and petrol are used together (complements). (ii) Demand for accessories falls along with the demand for cars (complements). (iii) Public transport demand rises, since people replace costly private driving by a cheaper alternative (substitute).
s: Petrol cars: fall, as complements
Accessories: fall, linked to demand for cars
Public transport: rise, as a cheaper substitute

questions.q: Tanvi finds the first mango delicious, the second good, and by the fourth she barely wants another, though the price has not moved. What does this mean for her demand, according to the chapter?
questions.a: The extra usefulness from each additional mango falls (diminishing marginal utility), so her willingness to pay falls and her demand for more mangoes falls.
o: Her willingness to pay falls, so demand for more mangoes falls
Her income has fallen, so she can no longer afford any more mangoes
Mangoes have turned into a complementary good for her at this price
Her demand for mangoes has risen because their supply has increased

questions.q: Srivalli likes mangoes and cannot replace them with oranges, even though oranges are cheaper. (a) Which factor affecting demand is this? (b) What does it show about how a fall in the orange price affects her demand for mangoes?
questions.a: (a) Taste and preference. (b) Her demand for mangoes does not fall just because oranges are cheaper, since she does not treat them as a replacement.
s: (a) Taste and preference
(b) The cheaper oranges do not take away her demand for mangoes

questions.q: A town has 12,000 residents of whom 30 per cent are children, 50 per cent working adults and 20 per cent elderly. (a) How many people are in each group? (b) Which footwear will the chapter say is most in demand among the largest group?
questions.a: (a) 3,600 children, 6,000 working adults, 2,400 elderly. (b) Working adults are the largest group, so formal shoes.
s: (a) The three group sizes worked out
(b) Largest group identified and linked to formal shoes

questions.q: Use the mango example to explain the principle of diminishing marginal utility. Then apply it to a second good of your choice and explain what it implies for a seller who wants one customer to buy more and more of the same item.
questions.a: With the first mango the taste is delicious, with the second still good, but by the third or fourth the buyer is barely interested: the additional usefulness falls as more is consumed. As the utility falls, willingness to pay falls, so demand falls. Second example: samosas at a fair; the fifth gives less satisfaction than the first. Implication: to sell more to the same customer the seller usually has to lower the price or offer something different, since willingness to pay for each extra unit is falling.
s: Mango example with falling additional usefulness
Link from falling utility to falling willingness to pay and demand
A correct second example
Implication for the seller

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A shop in a hill town sells many more sweaters in December than in July, even when its prices are the same in both months.
Reason (R): Demand for products changes through the year depending on weather, festivals and cultural habits rather than on the price of the good.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: seasonality shifts demand, as the chapter says of sweaters and jackets in winter, without any price change.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Name the factor at work in each case. (a) Bookshops are crowded at the beginning of the new academic session. (b) Families delay buying a refrigerator until just before Diwali. Then explain why demand changes in both cases though the price today does not.
questions.a: (a) Seasonality. (b) Future price expectations (expecting festival discounts). In both, demand moves because of time of year or what buyers expect, not because of a change in the current price.
s: (a) Seasonality and (b) future price expectations named
Explanation: the causes are the time of year and expectations, not today's price

questions.q:
An electronics shop in Jaipur sells 40 television sets of one model in an ordinary month at Rs 30,000 each. In the three weeks before Diwali, with the price still Rs 30,000, it sells only 15 sets. In Diwali week it gives a 25 per cent discount and sells 90 sets. Each set costs the shop Rs 18,000. The owner wonders whether to give the 25 per cent discount for the whole month instead, expecting to sell 110 sets in all.
(a) Which factor explains the fall to 15 sets in the three weeks before Diwali, though the price was unchanged?
(b) Find the discounted price and compare the revenue of Diwali week with that of an ordinary month.
(c) Find the total revenue for the month under the present plan and under the whole-month discount plan.
(d) Work out the profit under each plan and recommend one, saying what the other plan would have done better.
questions.a: (a) Future price expectations: buyers expecting festival discounts postponed purchases. (b) 25 per cent off Rs 30,000 is Rs 22,500; Diwali week revenue is 90 x 22,500 = Rs 20,25,000 against 40 x 30,000 = Rs 12,00,000 in an ordinary month. (c) Present plan: 15 x 30,000 + 90 x 22,500 = Rs 24,75,000; discount plan: 110 x 22,500 = Rs 24,75,000, the same. (d) Present plan profit 15 x 12,000 + 90 x 4,500 = Rs 5,85,000; discount plan 110 x 4,500 = Rs 4,95,000. The present plan earns Rs 90,000 more, but the discount plan sells five more sets and stops customers from waiting; either recommendation is fine with the trade-off named.
s: (a) Future price expectations
(b) Rs 22,500 and the revenue comparison Rs 20,25,000 against Rs 12,00,000
(c) Both revenues Rs 24,75,000
(d) Profits Rs 5,85,000 and Rs 4,95,000 with a reasoned recommendation

questions.q: Which of these would most likely raise the present demand for scooters in a town, with the scooters' price today unchanged?
questions.a: If consumers expect prices to rise, they buy immediately, which increases present demand even when current prices have not changed.
o: Buyers learn that prices will go up from next month
Buyers learn that a festival discount starts next week
Buyers learn that the factory will cut prices by a fifth next year
Buyers learn that the town's elderly share will fall

questions.a: Movie tickets and popcorn are complementary goods, used together. If tickets become dearer, fewer people go, so the demand for popcorn falls though its price is unchanged.
o: It falls, as popcorn is bought along with the ticket
It rises, as popcorn replaces the cinema for those who stay away
It stays the same, as the popcorn price is unchanged
It rises, as popcorn is a substitute for the film itself

questions.a: False. The chapter says market supply is the sum of all individual supplies, such as A + B + C, not their average.

questions.q: At Rs 50, Rs 100 and Rs 150 seller A offers 1, 2 and 3 kg and seller B offers 3, 4 and 7 kg. Find the market supply of these two sellers at each price and say whether the supply curve drawn from these figures slopes upward or downward.
questions.a: 4 kg at Rs 50, 6 kg at Rs 100 and 10 kg at Rs 150. The quantity rises with the price, so the curve slopes upward, as the Law of Supply says.

Quantity rises as price rises
Upward-sloping curve linked to the Law of Supply

questions.q: Compare the Law of Demand and the Law of Supply. Cover the direction of the relationship, the slope of the curve, the reason behind each and how the individual curve becomes the market curve, using figures from the mango tables.
questions.a: Demand: price and quantity demanded are inversely related, so the curve slopes downward; for Srivalli 1, 2, 3 kg at Rs 150, 100, 50. Supply: a direct relationship, so the curve slopes upward; for seller A 1, 2, 3 kg at Rs 50, 100, 150. Buyers buy more at lower prices; sellers supply more at higher prices because profit rises and new firms enter. Both market curves are got by adding the individual quantities at each price: 6, 12, 18 kg for the three buyers and for the three sellers.
s: Direction and slope of both curves
Reason behind each law
Adding individual to market, with figures

questions.q: A baker finds that when the price of cakes rises, she bakes more, and a neighbour who never sold cakes before starts doing so. Which pair of reasons from the chapter explains both changes?
questions.a: The chapter says a higher price raises profitability, which gives producers an incentive to produce more, and also attracts new firms to the market.
o: Higher profit tempts producers to make more and draws in new sellers
Higher prices lower the cost of making cakes and raise the number of buyers
Lower input costs help all bakers while the demand for cakes also falls
Cold storage raises her output and the government fixes the price of cakes

questions.q: Give the two reasons the chapter offers for the Law of Supply, that is, why a higher price leads sellers to supply more.
questions.a: A higher price increases profitability, which gives producers an incentive to raise output; and it attracts new firms to the market.
s: Higher profitability gives producers an incentive to produce more
A higher price attracts new firms to the market

questions.q: Gurmeet's farm can grow either wheat or chickpeas. This year wheat prices are low and chickpea prices are high, so he sows chickpeas on most of his land. Which factor affecting supply does this show?
questions.a: The chapter says the supply of one good depends on the profitability of other alternatives for the supplier: with low wheat and high chickpea prices he will grow more chickpeas.
o: The price of a related good he could grow instead
The number of sellers in the chickpea market

questions.q: Trace the market for face masks before, during and after the pandemic. At each stage say what happened to demand, supply and price, and justify the chapter's claim that the market 'never fully settles' at its previous equilibrium.
questions.a: Before: an equilibrium at a normal price. During: demand surged rapidly, supply could not catch up immediately, so the price rose significantly. Later: suppliers adjusted to the higher demand and the price fell. After: demand reduced further and the price went back to pre-pandemic levels. Justification: at each stage a new condition altered demand or supply, so the market was always moving towards a new equilibrium; even the return to the old price was a result of new changes, not a fixed position.
s: Demand, supply and price in the surge
Supplier adjustment and the fall in price
The return after the pandemic
Justification that the market keeps adjusting

questions.q: (a) Why did the price of face masks rise significantly in 2020? (b) Why did it fall again later, and to what level?
questions.a: (a) Demand surged and supply could not catch up immediately. (b) Suppliers adjusted to the increased demand, so prices fell; after the pandemic demand reduced and prices went back to pre-pandemic levels.
s: (a) Demand surge with supply lagging
(b) Suppliers adjusted, then demand reduced; prices returned to the pre-pandemic level

questions.q: True or False: In the real world, markets are always adjusting towards a new equilibrium and never fully settle at the previous one.
questions.a: True. Changes in technology, wages, interest rates, wars, pandemics, weather and disasters keep altering demand and supply, so equilibrium moves all the time.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: demand and supply keep being altered by changing conditions

questions.q:
A Goa hotel with 100 rooms has fixed Rs 8,000 a night for a December Saturday. A group tour cancels 30 rooms three days before. The manager can either cut the tariff of the 30 rooms by 40 per cent now and be sure of filling them, or wait for last-minute bookings at the full Rs 8,000. Past booking trends suggest only a 50 per cent chance that all 30 rooms would be sold at the full tariff if she waits, and nothing is earned from rooms left empty.
(a) What is the reduced tariff, and what would the 30 rooms bring in at it?
(b) What would they bring in if they all sold at the full tariff?
(c) Find the expected income from waiting, and say which option is better on money alone.
(d) Which two of the chapter's factors (for example, booking speed or days left) would you watch before deciding, and how would a 70 per cent chance change your advice?
questions.a: (a) 8,000 x 0.60 = Rs 4,800; 30 x 4,800 = Rs 1,44,000. (b) 30 x 8,000 = Rs 2,40,000. (c) Expected income from waiting is 0.5 x 2,40,000 = Rs 1,20,000, which is less than Rs 1,44,000, so cutting the tariff is better on money alone. (d) Any two of: how fast rooms are being booked, days left before arrival, past booking trends, nearby hotels' tariffs, events, weather. At a 70 per cent chance the expected income is 0.7 x 2,40,000 = Rs 1,68,000, which beats Rs 1,44,000, so waiting becomes the better choice; the break-even chance is 60 per cent.
s: (c) Expected Rs 1,20,000 and the better option stated
(d) Two chapter factors named and the effect of a 70 per cent chance

questions.q: Which of these is NOT given in the chapter as a limitation of government intervention in markets?
questions.a: The chapter gives price distortions with reduced producer incentives, compliance burdens and discouraging innovation. It does not say that intervention always makes every price rise.
o: It always raises the price of every good in the market
It can distort prices and reduce the incentive to produce
It can burden small businesses with permits and procedures
It can reduce the incentive to invest in new ideas

questions.q: (a) Name two kinds of permissions a small restaurant may need, according to the chapter. (b) Why may this discourage small entrepreneurs, and which limitation of intervention is this?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: food safety, fire safety, pollution control, local clearances. (b) The time and cost involved can discourage them from starting or expanding; this is the compliance burden.
s: (a) Two permissions named
(b) Time and cost discourage; compliance burden named

questions.q:
Read these statements about the role of government in markets.
1. A price ceiling is a maximum price, for example one set for medicines to prevent overcharging.
2. A monopoly can charge higher prices and supply less than a competitive market would.
3. Roads and street lighting are usually provided by private companies because they bring direct profit.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statement 3 is false: public goods like roads are usually not provided by private companies because they do not generate direct profit, so the government provides them. Statements 1 and 2 are from the chapter.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Use the sanitiser example to explain why the government stepped in during COVID-19, what it did, and what happened. Then argue both sides of the chapter's question: should such price controls stay for ever?
questions.a: Demand surged, causing stockouts and sharp price rises, and some shopkeepers began hoarding and black marketing. The government declared sanitisers essential commodities under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 and capped the retail price of 200 ml at Rs 100. Companies started production and sanitisers became widely available at fair prices. For permanent control: protection of low-income buyers from overcharging. Against: controls below market levels distort prices, reduce producers' incentives and may lead to shortages and less innovation; the cap was meant for an emergency.
s: Why the government stepped in
What it did, with the Act and the cap
The outcome
An argument for permanence and one against, from the chapter

questions.q: Explain why public goods are usually provided by the government. Use three examples from the chapter and the Rs 5,000 per family park example to show what goes wrong if provision is left to private payment.
questions.a: Public goods are provided for the benefit of all citizens, e.g. roads, bridges, parks, street lighting, defence, sanitation and drainage. Private companies usually do not provide them because they do not generate direct profit. In the park example, each family may think others will pay and it can use the park free, so too little is collected and the park is never built though all need it. This is why such goods need government provision or funding for social welfare, development and equal access.
s: Meaning of public goods and three examples
Why private companies do not provide them
The park example and what goes wrong
The conclusion on government provision

questions.q: The government fixes a maximum price of Rs 20 per kg for wheat while the market-driven price is Rs 30 per kg. Which outcome does the chapter expect?
questions.a: Farmers then receive less than they would in a free market, may lose motivation to produce, and this may lead to reduced production and shortages.
o: Lower production and shortages, as farmers get less than market price
Higher production, as farmers are paid a price fixed for them
A surplus of wheat, as the price is below what buyers expected
No change, since the price the government fixed is the equilibrium price

questions.q: Sima says, 'The Rs 100 cap on a 200 ml bottle of sanitiser worked well in the emergency, so such price controls should be kept in force for ever.' How far is she right?
questions.a: Partly right. The cap was imposed in an emergency; sanitisers soon became widely available at fair prices, so it helped. But the chapter warns that controls below market levels distort prices and reduce producers' incentive to supply, and it asks whether such controls should stay for ever, so permanence goes beyond what it supports.
s: Verdict: partly right
The right part: the cap helped in the emergency
The limits: price distortions and reduced incentives make permanence doubtful

questions.q: Aman says, 'A government should step in only when prices rise too high; if prices fall, the market is working fairly and nothing needs doing.' Is he right? Use the chapter's examples.
questions.a: Partly. A price ceiling (as on sanitisers in a shortage) protects buyers from a very high price. But the chapter also gives the price floor (a minimum wage), because a price that falls too low harms sellers, such as workers selling their labour. So intervention can be needed in both directions.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: a ceiling protects buyers from very high prices
Flaw: a floor protects sellers when the price falls too low, as with a minimum wage

questions.q: (a) Give two ways in which, according to the chapter, a monopoly can harm consumers. (b) What does the government do about it?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: higher prices, poorer quality of goods and services, restricted supply. (b) It regulates such practices by keeping the prices and the quantity supplied in check.
s: (a) Two harms named
(b) Regulation of prices and quantity supplied

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A small restaurateur may hesitate to start or expand a business even when the demand for her food is rising.
Reason (R): Government intervention often requires licences, permits and compliance procedures whose time and cost can discourage small entrepreneurs.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: the chapter's example is a small restaurant that needs food-safety, fire-safety, pollution-control and local clearances.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: If the government fixes a maximum price of Rs 20 per kg for wheat while the market-driven price is Rs 30, a farmer gets Rs ___ less on every kilogram sold.

A colony needs a park that costs Rs 4,00,000, and each family is asked for Rs 5,000. (a) How many families must pay? (b) Only 60 families pay. Find the money collected and the shortfall, and say what this suggests about goods that benefit everyone.
questions.a: (a) 4,00,000 / 5,000 = 80 families. (b) 60 x 5,000 = Rs 3,00,000 collected, a shortfall of Rs 1,00,000. Goods that benefit everyone are often under-provided if left to voluntary payment, so government provision or funding is required.
s: (a) 80 families
(b) Rs 3,00,000 collected, shortfall Rs 1,00,000, linked to the need for government funding

questions.q: A customer wants to complain about unfair trade practices by a seller, and a bank depositor wants to know which authority supervises banks. (a) Name the regulator for each case. (b) What does the chapter say regulators ensure in the market?
questions.a: (a) The Central Consumer Protection Authority for the unfair trade practice, and the Reserve Bank of India for banking. (b) They ensure transparency in the market.
s: (a) The CCPA for unfair practices and the RBI for banking
(b) Transparency in the market

questions.q:
A ward has 120 families who need a park costing Rs 6,00,000, so each family was asked for Rs 5,000. Only 90 families paid. The municipality has Rs 3,00,000 in its budget. It can either cover the shortfall for the park, which 120 families would use, or repair the streetlights on the ward's roads, which costs Rs 2,00,000 and would serve 400 families. It cannot do both.
(a) How much was collected and how large is the shortfall?
(b) Why, according to the chapter, did some families not pay, and what does this show about public goods?
(c) Work out the cost per family served of each project.
(d) Which project should the municipality fund? Justify your choice and say who loses out.
questions.a: (a) 90 x 5,000 = Rs 4,50,000 collected, a shortfall of Rs 1,50,000. (b) Families may think that if others pay the park will be built anyway and they can use it without paying; goods that benefit everyone often need government provision or funding. (c) Park shortfall Rs 1,50,000 / 120 = Rs 1,250 per family; streetlights Rs 2,00,000 / 400 = Rs 500 per family. (d) The streetlights serve more people at a lower cost per family, while funding the park completes a project 90 families have already paid for. Either is acceptable if the loser is named: the other project stays unfunded, since the remaining budget (Rs 1,50,000 or Rs 1,00,000) falls short of the other's cost.
s: (a) Rs 4,50,000 and a shortfall of Rs 1,50,000
(b) Thinking that others will pay, and the need for government funding of public goods
(c) Rs 1,250 and Rs 500 per family
(d) A justified choice that names who loses out

questions.q: During a sudden shortage, a shopkeeper buys up 500 bottles of sanitiser and keeps them locked in his godown, planning to sell them later when prices are higher. Which term from the chapter describes what he is doing?
questions.a: Hoarding is the accumulation of goods beyond what is immediately necessary, driven by anticipated price increases or fear of shortages.
o: Hoarding
Price floor
Monopoly
Public provision

questions.q: In a town the market-clearing wage for farm helpers is Rs 400 a day. The government sets a minimum wage of Rs 350 a day. What does the chapter's idea of a price floor tell us about this rule?
questions.a: The chapter says a price floor is effective only if it is set above the market equilibrium price. A floor of Rs 350 below the equilibrium of Rs 400 would not change the wage.
o: It has no effect, since it is below the equilibrium wage
It raises every wage in the town to Rs 350 straight away
It creates a shortage of farm helpers throughout the town
It works as a price ceiling on the wage that employers pay

questions.q: True or False: A price floor set below the market equilibrium price will be effective in raising the price.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that for a price floor to be effective it must be set above the market equilibrium price; a floor below it changes nothing.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a floor works only if it is set above the equilibrium price

questions.q: Before the government's cap, sanitiser in a town sold at Rs 160 for 200 ml. The cap is Rs 100. (a) Find a family's saving on 6 bottles. (b) Find the capped price per millilitre. (c) Name the two practices that the chapter says some shopkeepers adopted when stocks ran out.
questions.a: (a) 6 x (160 - 100) = Rs 360. (b) 100 / 200 = Rs 0.50 per ml. (c) Hoarding and black marketing.
s: (a) A saving of Rs 360
(b) Rs 0.50 per ml
(c) Hoarding and black marketing

questions.q: A neighbourhood needs a park that many families would use. Each family thinks, 'If the others pay, the park will be built anyway, and I can use it without paying.' What does the chapter say follows from this thinking?
questions.a: Not enough money is collected and the park is never built, though everyone needs it; so goods that benefit everyone often need government provision or funding.

The park is built quickly, since every family waits for the others to pay
The park is built by a private company that earns profit from it
The park is built by the families paying equal shares without difficulty

questions.q:
A state sets a maximum price of Rs 20 per kg for wheat, to keep flour affordable, while the market-driven price is Rs 30. A farmer, Hardev, grows 6,000 kg of wheat in a season and spends Rs 24 on every kilogram. He is thinking of using his savings to buy better seeds and drip irrigation, which would raise his yield.
(a) Work out Hardev's profit for the season at the maximum price and at the market price.
(b) Which limitation of government intervention from the chapter does this show, and what is the likely effect on his production?
(c) What does the chapter say about his plan to buy better seeds and irrigation?
(d) The government wants poorer families to buy flour cheaply, yet wants farmers to keep producing. Advise on keeping, removing or changing the cap, and name what your advice gives up.
questions.a: (a) At Rs 20 he loses 6,000 x 4 = Rs 24,000; at Rs 30 he gains 6,000 x 6 = Rs 36,000. (b) Price distortions and reduced producer incentives: farmers receive less than the free-market price, may lose motivation and reduce production, leading to shortages. (c) Without adequate returns he is unlikely to invest in better seeds or irrigation, which reduces long-term productivity and output. (d) Any reasoned advice: keeping the cap helps poorer buyers now but risks shortages and lower investment; removing it restores incentives but raises flour prices for the poor; a middle course might protect only the poor. The advice must name what is given up.
s: (a) Loss of Rs 24,000 and profit of Rs 36,000
(b) Price distortions and reduced incentive, with lower production
(c) No investment in better seeds, so lower long-term output
(d) A reasoned recommendation naming what is given up
